query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In an initially single‐phase, compositionally complex high‐entropy alloy, exposure to service‐relevant thermal and mechanical loads activates nanoscale diffusion that leads to the gradual nanoclustering of principal elements at grain boundaries, thereby reducing interfacial cohesion and triggering a brittle transition that is distinct from conventional segregation or intermetallic precipitation mechanisms.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase compositionally complex HEA (e.g., equiatomic FCC alloy such as CrMnFeCoNi) with a homogeneous grain-boundary chemistry and no detectable grain-boundary segregation or intermetallic formation.
generation.intervention: Apply a series of controlled thermal aging (annealing) treatments combined with specified levels of mechanical loading (either static or cyclic stress) to simulate service conditions.
generation.conditions: Temperature exposures ranging from moderate to high service temperatures and mechanical loading at varying strain rates that are representative of engineering service; the protocol should include both low-temperature (to rule out conventional embrittlement) and elevated temperature conditions to activate diffusion.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoclusters enriched in one or more of the principal elements (e.g., Cr, Ni, Mn) that form at grain boundaries under activated conditions.
generation.mechanism: Thermal and stress-driven activation enhances local atomic mobility at grain boundaries, initiating nanoscale clustering that depletes cohesive bonding at these interfaces. This reduced cohesion facilitates intergranular fracture and brittle behavior, even in the absence of conventional grain-boundary segregation or precipitate formation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated state, the treated HEA will exhibit a measurable decrease in fracture toughness and a shift to more brittle failure modes, correlated with the appearance and increased density of nanoclusters at grain boundaries as detected by high-resolution techniques.
generation.baseline: The as-homogenized HEA state showing high toughness, ductile deformation behavior, and uniform grain-boundary chemistry without nanoclustering.
generation.boundary: The brittle transition is expected only when service conditions (temperature and stress) exceed a threshold that promotes significant grain-boundary nanoclustering; below this threshold, the alloy should maintain its ductile, tough behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The precise threshold of temperature, stress level, and exposure time required to initiate nanoclustering is not yet well-defined and may vary with alloy composition and microstructural factors.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a controlled-variable experiment where identical HEA samples are subjected to different combinations of thermal aging (e.g., at 600°C, 700°C, 800°C) and applied mechanical loads (both static and cyclic stress) for varying durations. Use in situ high-resolution characterization (atom probe tomography and transmission electron microscopy) to assess grain-boundary chemistry evolution in parallel with mechanical testing (fracture toughness and tensile tests). Include a conventional alloy control sample that is known to degrade via grain-boundary segregation and intermetallic formation.
measurements: Quantitative fracture toughness (KJIc) and tensile ductility measurements before and after treatment.
High-resolution imaging and atom probe tomography to detect and quantify nanoclustering at grain boundaries.
Comparison of the onset of brittleness with changes in grain-boundary chemistry and microstructural features.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If samples subjected to the imposed thermal and mechanical conditions exhibit significant loss in toughness and a transition to brittle behavior without any observable formation of nanoscale clusters at the grain boundaries, then the proposed mechanism of nanoclustering as the primary trigger for brittle transition is falsified.

frame.goal: To understand and explain the mechanistic origin of toughness degradation (or brittle behavior) in these HEAs, and to identify under what conditions brittle behavior emerges compared to conventional alloys.
frame.limitation: The current findings in HEAs do not establish what governs toughness degradation in an initially single-phase alloy, especially given their suppression of conventional degradation mechanisms like grain-boundary segregation and intermetallic precipitation.

frame.regime: Controlled testing should span service-relevant conditions, including high-temperature exposure (to assess resistance to softening) and low-temperature conditions (to check for embrittlement), under mechanical loading conditions that mirror those in engineering applications.

decision.trend: Early studies in conventional alloys linked toughness degradation to bulk mechanisms like grain-boundary segregation and intermetallic precipitation. In HEAs, initial work confirmed outstanding strength‐toughness performance and microstructural stability, ruling out those conventional degradation paths. Subsequent studies (e.g., PMC6897545) then revealed that even in a nominally single‐phase HEA, nanometer‐scale segregation (or nanoclustering) of principal elements at the grain boundaries can reduce interfacial cohesion and trigger brittle failure. Research has thus progressed from documenting superior performance to uncovering subtle, nanoscale phenomena that might compromise toughness under specific conditions.
decision.unsolved: What remains unknown is the precise mechanistic trigger – under service-relevant thermal and mechanical conditions – that initiates nanoclustering at grain boundaries in an initially homogeneous HEA, leading to an abrupt loss of toughness. In particular, there is no controlled experimental framework yet that distinguishes this mechanism from conventional alloy behavior by systematically varying relevant parameters such as temperature, stress state, and time in service.
decision.lever: Systematic variation of thermal and mechanical loading conditions (e.g., controlled aging/annealing under defined stress and temperature profiles) combined with high-resolution characterization (atom probe tomography and in situ microscopy) to monitor onset and evolution of nanoclustering at grain boundaries
decision.why: Following the trend from establishing superior HEA performance to identifying subtle nanoclustering as a ductility-limiting factor, the next logical step is a controlled experiment that isolates the kinetics of nanoclustering. By adjusting key service parameters and directly comparing the grain boundary chemistry evolution in HEAs versus conventional alloys, this approach can decisively test the hypothesis that thermally and stress-activated grain boundary nanoclustering governs the brittle transition in an otherwise single-phase, compositionally complex alloy.
